Injectivity on one line

by Janusz Gwoździewicz Address: Department of Mathematics,Technical University,Al. 1000 LPP 7, 25–314 Kielce, Poland
Abstract

Let kk be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Let H:k2→k2H:k^{2}\to k^{2} be a polynomial mapping such that the Jacobian Jac⁡H\operatorname{Jac}H is a non-zero constant. In this note we prove, that if there is a line l⊂k2l\subset k^{2} such that H|l:l→k2H|_{l}:l\to k^{2} is an injection, then HH is a polynomial automorphism.

1. Main result

Let kk be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Put k∗=k∖{0}k^{*}=k\setminus\{0\}. By Aut⁡k2\operatorname{Aut}k^{2} we denote the group of polynomial automorphisms i.e. all mappings H=(f,g):k2→k2H=(f,g):k^{2}\to k^{2}, ff, g∈k⁡[x,y]g\in k[x,y] for which there exists an inverse polynomial mapping. Remind that for H∈Aut⁡k2H\in\operatorname{Aut}k^{2} the Jacobian Jac⁡H\operatorname{Jac}H is a non-zero constant. The famous Keller conjecture states that any polynomial mapping which has the non-zero constant Jacobian is a polynomial automorphism.

Theorem~1.1

Let H:k2→k2H:k^{2}\to k^{2} be a polynomial mapping such that Jac⁡H∈k∗\operatorname{Jac}H\in k^{*}. If there exists a line l⊂k2l\subset k^{2} such that H|l:l→k2H|_{l}:l\to k^{2} is injective then HH is a polynomial automorphism.

The proof of the above theorem is given in Section 2 of this note. Let us note here that a weaker result (injectivity on three lines) has been proved recently in [4].

2. Proof of the theorem

The proof of our result is based on the Abhyankar–Moh theorem and on some properties of Newton’s polygon which we quote below.

If ff is a polynomial in k⁡[x,y]k[x,y] then SfS_{f} denotes the support of ff, that is, SfS_{f} is the set of integer points (i,j)(i,j) such that the monomial xi​yjx^{i}y^{j} appears in ff with a non-zero coefficient. We denote by NfN_{f} the convex hull (in the real space R2R^{2}) of Sf∪{(0,0)}S_{f}\cup\{(0,0)\}. The set NfN_{f} is called (see [2]) Newton’s polygon of ff.

Theorem 2.1

([2], [3, theorem~3.4.]) Let ff, gg be polynomials in k⁡[x,y]k[x,y]. Assume that Jac⁡(f,g)\operatorname{Jac}(f,g) is a non-zero constant and deg⁡f>1\deg f>1, deg⁡g>1\deg g>1. Then the polygons NfN_{f} and NgN_{g} are similar, that is Ng=deg⁡gdeg⁡f​NfN_{g}=\frac{\deg g}{\deg f}N_{f}.

The following lemma is easy to check, so we omit the proof.

Lemma 2.2

Let ff, gg be polynomials in k⁡[x,y]k[x,y] with Jac⁡(f,g)∈k∗\operatorname{Jac}(f,g)\in k^{*}. If deg⁡f≤1\deg f\leq 1 or deg⁡g≤1\deg g\leq 1 then the mapping (f,g)(f,g) is a polynomial automorphism.

Lemma 2.3

Let H=(f,g)H=(f,g) be a polynomial mapping such that Jac⁡H\operatorname{Jac}H is a non-zero constant. If H⁡(x,0)=(x,0)H(x,0)=(x,0) then H∈Aut⁡k2H\in\operatorname{Aut}k^{2}.

Proof

First suppose that deg⁡f>1\deg f>1, deg⁡g>1\deg g>1. We have

f⁡(x,0)=x\displaystyle f(x,0)=x 12
g⁡(x,0)=0.\displaystyle g(x,0)=0.

From (1) the point (1,0)(1,0) belongs to the polygon NfN_{f}, so by theorem 2.1 (deg⁡gdeg⁡f,0)∈Ng(\frac{\deg g}{\deg f},0)\in N_{g}. This means that the polynomial gg contains some monomials of the form xix^{i}, i>0i>0 with non-zero coefficients but this is a cotradiction with (2).

We have deg⁡f≤1\deg f\leq 1 or deg⁡g≤1\deg g\leq 1 and by lemma 2.2 HH is a polynomial automorphism.

Proof of theorem~1.1

Without loss of generality we may assume that the line ll has an equation y=0y=0. Otherwiese we replace HH by H∘LH\circ L where LL is an affine automorphism such that L({y=0})=lL(\{y=0\})=l.

Put γ⁡(x)=H⁡(x,0)\gamma(x)=H(x,0). By assumptions of the theorem the mapping γ:k→k2\gamma:k\to k^{2} is an injection and γ′​(x)≠0\gamma^{\prime}(x)\neq 0 for x∈kx\in k, hence γ\gamma is an embedding of the line in the plane. By Abhyankar-Moh theorem [1] there exist an automorphism H1∈Aut⁡k2H_{1}\in\operatorname{Aut}k^{2} such that γ⁡(x)=H1​(x,0)\gamma(x)=H_{1}(x,0). Let G=H1∘HG=H_{1}\circ H. We get Jac⁡G=Jac⁡H1−1​Jac⁡H\operatorname{Jac}G=\operatorname{Jac}H_{1}^{-1}\operatorname{Jac}H is a non-zero constant and G⁡(x,0)=(x,0)G(x,0)=(x,0), so by lemma 2.3 G∈Aut⁡k2G\in\operatorname{Aut}k^{2}. Therefore H=H1∘GH=H_{1}\circ G is a polynomial automorphism.
